\chapter{¡Qué Grande! --- The Same Word, Exclaiming}
\label{ch:que-grande}
\hlchaptermodality{248}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can react to something with force, in two words.}

I can react to something with force, in two words.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[¡Qué grande!]{¡Qué grande! — the same word, exclaiming}

\label{lesson:ES-C64-que-grande}



\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Qué es esto?} asks. And you have had the upside-down exclamation mark since the writing chapters, with nothing much to put between the pair.

Here is what goes there.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: qué in front of an adjective}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{¡Qué grande!}} — How big! \emph{\textbf{¡Qué bien!}} — How good! / Great!
\end{quote}

No verb needed, nothing else needed. \emph{Qué} plus an adjective or an adverb, between the two marks, and you have said something with force.

\emph{¡Qué bien!} in particular is worth having on the tip of your tongue. It is what Spanish says when English says \emph{nice!} or \emph{great!}, and it costs two words.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Notice the accent. It is there in \emph{¿qué?} and it is here in \emph{¡qué!}, and by now you know why: that mark has never been about questions. It marks the word \textbf{carrying the force} of the sentence.

You saw the same thing when a reported question kept its accent inside a sentence with no question marks at all. Asking and exclaiming are two jobs, and the accent is the one thing they share.

Plain \emph{que} — no accent — is the joint you use for reporting and for relative clauses. It carries nothing, so it is marked with nothing.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{¡Qué grande!}, \emph{¡Qué bien!}
  \item \emph{¿qué?} then \emph{¡qué!}, and hear that only the frame changed
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What follows \emph{qué} in an exclamation? (An \textbf{adjective} or an adverb — no verb needed.)

And does it keep its accent? (\textbf{Yes} — it is still the word doing the work.)
\end{tcolorbox}
